worker_target_description: Study 1, section 4.4: Pearson correlation of all PythonTA errors remaining in a final graded Python submission with percentage of correctness tests failed. This is the conceptual replication of the overall-grades/all-static-analysis-errors relationship, explicitly contrasted with the original in the same paragraph.
worker_notes: Only assigned unfinished fields were evaluated; original is an unassigned placeholder. Same-test p < .001 retained with the printed R = −0.53. Preserve the printed negative sign despite the text describing percentage of correctness tests failed. The separate Coding Flaws correlation R = −0.54 is not this target. Table 1 prints 1270 participants, 34629 interim submissions, and 15060 final submissions; these are corpus counts, with no explicit N attached to the critical Pearson test. Section 4.4 continues on p. 84 with G1/G2/G3 counts 2086, 726, 641 for a distinct grouped coding-flaw correctness analysis; these were not summed or transferred to the all-errors correlation. No N derived from df. Authors provide a general paper-level verdict (Our findings are generally consistent with the Edwards et al. study, ... though with some notable differences.), but no explicit success/failure verdict for the assigned all-errors correlation; significance alone was not converted into replication success.

coding_context.reported_success_quote:
We confirm that almost a decade
later and even after being instructed to use the auto-formatting
options within their IDE, students still encounter mostly formatting errors when using a static analysis tool. We find that the second-
most common category of errors detected are “Coding Flaws”, and,
like Edwards et al., that the frequency of coding flaws identified by the static analysis tool correlates to program correctness.
